text: Chapter two moves from the portal into code. First stop: the basics of the Azure AI Foundry SDK.

Three packages cover most of what you'll need. Azure-identity handles authentication. Azure-ai-projects is the project-level client for deployments, connections, and agents. And either the OpenAI SDK or azure-ai-inference is what actually sends your chat requests.

Every one of those clients needs two things: an endpoint URL and credentials. Your project's Overview page in the Foundry portal shows both — this is where you'll come back to whenever a client won't connect.

In code, you create a DefaultAzureCredential and pass it, along with your project's endpoint, into an AIProjectClient. DefaultAzureCredential tries your Azure CLI login, a managed identity, or environment variables, in that order — so no raw key ever sits in your source code.

From the project client, get_openai_client hands you back a client with the exact same shape as the standard OpenAI SDK. You call chat.completions.create, pass your deployment name as the model, and read the reply the same way you would anywhere else.

If a deployment name throws a 404, the fix is almost always here: the Models and endpoints page lists every deployment that actually exists in your project, so you can confirm the exact name your code should be calling.
With authentication and a basic call working, next we do a full deployment from scratch — picking a model, deploying it, and wiring up the endpoint ourselves.
